## Your Python so far {.scrollable}

The 57 names below came out of sessions 2–10. Today's slides assume them, and add to them. The ones marked are the newest, from session 10.

### Load and shape

- `.dropna` — drop rows with missing values
- `.merge` — join two frames on a key
- `.shape` — rows and columns
- `pd.read_parquet` — a parquet file, directly
- `qmib.load` — a course dataset, by name
- `pd.get_dummies` — categories to indicator columns
- `StandardScaler` — standardise before you penalise
- `make_pipeline` — so the scaler is fitted on train only
- `pd.concat` — stack the matched sample back together · *new in session 10*

### Describe

- `.mean / .median` — the two centres, and their gap
- `.quantile` — any quantile, including the median
- `.std / .var` — spread, dividing by $n-1$
- `stats.trim_mean` — the mean after cutting both tails
- `.value_counts` — how unbalanced is the outcome
- `pd.crosstab` — a contingency table in one call
- `np.cov` — the matrix the model is trying to reproduce

### Fit

- `.fit()` — estimate the model you specified
- `smf.ols` — least squares, from a formula
- `OrderedModel` — ordered categories, proportional odds
- `sm.MNLogit` — unordered categories, one baseline
- `sm.add_constant` — the intercept, when there is no formula
- `smf.logit` — binary outcome, from a formula
- `Ridge / Lasso / ElasticNet` — the three penalties
- `semopy.Model` — from a model description string
- `expit` — the inverse logit, when you need it directly · *new in session 10*

### Read the fit

- `.params` — the coefficients, in units of $y$
- `.rsquared` — share of variance explained
- `.mse_resid` — its square root is the RSE, in units
- `.resid / .fittedvalues` — what is left, and what was predicted
- `.rsquared_adj` — penalised for the extra predictor
- `.get_prediction` — with an interval, via `.summary_frame()`
- `.predict` — fitted probabilities, not classes
- `np.exp` — a log-odds becomes an odds ratio
- `.coef_ / .alpha_` — scikit-learn's spelling of `.params`
- `.inspect()` — loadings and paths, estimated

### Diagnose

- `.cooks_distance` — influence: leverage $\times$ residual
- `.get_influence()` — the whole diagnostic bundle
- `.hat_matrix_diag` — leverage; sums to $p$, always
- `.resid_studentized_internal` — residuals on a common scale

### Choose and validate

- `.aic / .bic` — compare non-nested models
- `.llf` — log-likelihood, for the LR test
- `stats.chi2.sf` — the $p$-value of that test
- `KFold` — and do it $k$ times
- `RidgeCV / LassoCV / ElasticNetCV` — $\lambda$ by cross-validation
- `lasso_path` — the whole coefficient path
- `mean_squared_error` — score it on the held-out part
- `np.logspace` — a grid that is even in $\log\lambda$
- `train_test_split` — hold something back
- `semopy.calc_stats` — CFI, TLI, RMSEA — report all three
- `.kneighbors` — who got matched to whom · *new in session 10*
- `NearestNeighbors` — match treated to control · *new in session 10*

### Plot

- `plt.scatter` — the data, before anything else
- `plt.xlabel / plt.ylabel` — say the units, every time
- `plt.axhline / plt.axvline` — draw the threshold you are judging against
- `plt.stem` — one spike per observation
- `plt.subplots` — several panels, one figure
- `.boxplot` — balance, before and after matching · *new in session 10*

# 1 · The question we started with {background-color="#16181A" style="color:#F7F6F3"}

### Twelve weeks later, it is still the question

## Session 1 asked one thing

> When can a number about the past be used to make a claim about the future?

Every method since has been an answer to some version of it, and **every answer came with
conditions attached**.

::: {.check}
The methods will be looked up again. The conditions will not. That is why the conditions are the
thing worth carrying out of this room.
:::

## The sentence the course has been making

::: {.tight}
A quantitative result is an **argument**, and the arithmetic is only its smallest part.
:::

What makes a number worth acting on is the case that can be made for the conditions under which it
means what it appears to mean.

::: {.warn}
That case is constructed by the analyst. It is not computed by the software.
:::

# 2 · Five things that kept happening {background-color="#16181A" style="color:#F7F6F3"}

### Not five techniques — five recurring facts

## One · The arithmetic never refuses

::: {.tight}
- The normal equations return coefficients for **any** numbers you feed them
- Logistic regression on separated data runs its coefficients to infinity — and reports a large
  number, not an error
- Nearest neighbours predicts confidently **outside** the range of its training data
- A structural equation model fits the covariance matrix implied by an **entirely wrong** causal
  diagram
:::

::: {.warn}
A misspecified model does not raise an exception. It returns four decimal places in the same
typeface as a correct one.
:::

## Which is why diagnostics are a discipline

Not a formality, and not a box to tick after the interesting work is done.

::: {.check}
"The model says" is never a complete sentence.
:::

## Two · The same data answer differently

Session 6, on one dataset and one pair of variables:

| Specification | Estimate |
|---|---|
| Pooled | 1,111 |
| Country effects | 275 |
| Country **and** year effects | 1,149 |

Each was correct for the question its identifying variation could answer. A reader shown any one
alone would draw a different conclusion.

## And it was not an isolated case

::: {.tight}
- Session 2 — the slope fell **26%** when two controls were added, because "controlling for" is
  literally a residual regression
- Session 7 — the first component explained **97.5%** or **47%** of variance, depending only on
  whether the columns had been standardised
- Session 10 — the estimate ran from **+6.07** to **+2.68**, depending on whether selection was
  addressed
:::

::: {.warn}
A coefficient is meaningless without the specification that produced it. Reporting one without the
other is reporting half a result.
:::

## Three · Fit does not identify structure

::: {.tight}
- Session 7 — a factor solution and its rotation fit **identically to eight decimal places**, while
  telling different stories
- Session 9 — two structural models with **opposite causal arrows** returned identical $\chi^2$,
  identical degrees of freedom, identical CFI, identical AIC
- Session 3 — four datasets shared every summary statistic and differed completely
:::

## The data were silent between the alternatives

The choice was made by the analyst, on grounds **outside** the data.

::: {.check}
That is not a defect to be engineered away. It is the permanent condition of empirical work.
:::

The honest response is to **name the alternative you rejected, and say why** — which is a different
activity from reporting a fit index.

## Four · Flexibility is a purchase, not a virtue

Session 5 introduced a deliberately **biased** estimator and watched it beat the unbiased one,
because unbiasedness is worth nothing if the variance is large enough.

Session 8 made the trade explicit and then measured it: squared bias, variance and irreducible
error summing to test error at every $k$, with a minimum somewhere in the middle.

## Then session 8 sent itself the bill

On real data, nearest neighbours scored an **AUC of 0.51** — a coin flip — where logistic
regression, the rigid method with the strong assumption, reached **0.68**.

::: {.warn}
On accuracy alone, the comparison would have shown all methods identical and concluded that nothing
worked.
:::

::: {.check}
Complexity has to be justified against a simpler alternative that was **actually fitted**. Not
against an imagined one.
:::

## Five · Selection is the problem

In session 10 the naive comparison overstated a known effect of **+2.4 percentage points** by more
than **150%** — because the countries that adopted the policy were already different.

::: {.warn}
Nothing in the fit statistics of that naive comparison would have suggested a problem.
:::

That gap is the reason for matching, balance diagnostics, parallel trends and event studies — none
of which removes the need for an argument about **why** treatment arrived where it did.

# 3 · What we could check {background-color="#16181A" style="color:#F7F6F3"}

### And what no course can check for you

## Some things are not opinions

Because the course data are fixtures generated from a known structure, several claims could be
**verified** rather than asserted.

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| code-summary: "Three identities, one last time"

core = qmib.load("core").dropna(
    subset=["gdp_pc_eur", "productivity_idx", "employment_ths", "population"])
y = core["gdp_pc_eur"]

# 1. Pythagoras (session 2). The residual is orthogonal to the fit, so the
#    sums of squares add exactly — not approximately.
fit = sm.OLS(y, sm.add_constant(core[["productivity_idx"]])).fit()
tss = ((y - y.mean()) ** 2).sum()
ess = ((fit.fittedvalues - y.mean()) ** 2).sum()
rss = (fit.resid ** 2).sum()

# 2. Frisch-Waugh-Lovell (session 2). "Controlling for" IS residual regression.
others = sm.add_constant(core[["employment_ths", "population"]])
multi = sm.OLS(y, sm.add_constant(
    core[["productivity_idx", "employment_ths", "population"]])).fit()
fwl = sm.OLS(sm.OLS(y, others).fit().resid,
             sm.OLS(core["productivity_idx"], others).fit().resid).fit()

# 3. Leverage (session 3). The hat matrix diagonal sums to the number of
#    parameters. Always. For every regression ever fitted.
X = sm.add_constant(core[["productivity_idx"]]).to_numpy()
h = np.einsum("ij,jk,ik->i", X, np.linalg.inv(X.T @ X), X)

print(f"{'identity':44}{'discrepancy':>14}")
print(f"{'TSS - (ESS + RSS)':44}{tss - ess - rss:14.3e}")
print(f"{'multiple regression - FWL slope':44}"
      f"{abs(multi.params['productivity_idx'] - fwl.params.iloc[0]):14.3e}")
print(f"{'sum of leverages - p':44}{abs(h.sum() - X.shape[1]):14.3e}")
```

::: {.check}
These are algebraic identities. They hold for every regression, on every dataset, forever.
:::

## The failures were more instructive

::: {.tight}
- The lasso retained **three pure-noise columns** out of ten after cross-validated selection
- Regression adjustment on proxy covariates left **0.7 percentage points** of bias
- A measurement model taken from an exploratory factor solution failed **every** fit index
- A post-treatment control moved an estimate **closer to the truth** while being methodologically wrong
:::

## That last one is the course's most useful result

::: {.tight}
Being closer to the right answer is not the same as using the right method.
:::

::: {.warn}
Outside a textbook, you never learn which one you had.
:::

## A standing caveat

The course data in `data/spine/` are **teaching fixtures**, generated from a known structure with a
fixed seed. They are not observations of Europe.

::: {.warn}
Every number quoted in these twelve weeks is a fact about a simulation, not a fact about the world.
Do not cite one in a paper. The *reasoning* transfers; the *numbers* do not.
:::

# 4 · Why this matters in private organisations {background-color="#16181A" style="color:#F7F6F3"}

### Where the estimate meets a decision with money on it

## The firm's questions are this course's questions

| The decision | The session it belongs to |
|---|---|
| Should we enter this market, and what happens if we do? | 10, 11 — effects, not correlations |
| Which of forty indicators actually predicts default? | 5, 8 — selection and the bias–variance trade |
| Did the pricing change work, or did the market move? | 11 — difference-in-differences |
| What is "brand strength", and can we measure it? | 7, 9 — latent constructs |
| Which countries behave alike for planning purposes? | 6, 7 — structure across a panel |

## What a manager is actually buying from you

Not a model. **A defensible answer, and an honest account of its limits.**

::: {.tight}
- A point estimate with **no interval** cannot be planned against
- A coefficient with **no units** cannot be checked against what the business already knows
- A result with **no named assumption** cannot be revisited when conditions change
:::

::: {.check}
The most expensive analytical failures in business are not arithmetic errors. They are confident
answers to questions the data could not address.
:::

## The asymmetry that should govern your caution

::: {.tight}
- A model that is **wrong and uncertain** gets challenged
- A model that is **wrong and confident** gets implemented
:::

::: {.warn}
Your job includes making sure the second case is not you.
:::

# 5 · Why this matters in public organisations {background-color="#16181A" style="color:#F7F6F3"}

### Where the stakes are different in kind, not degree

## Public decisions raise the bar

A firm that misprices a product loses money and adjusts. A ministry that misreads an evaluation
**sets a policy that affects people who did not choose it**, and often cannot adjust for years.

::: {.tight}
- The counterfactual is rarely available — programmes are not randomly assigned
- The people affected are not the people who chose
- The decision is **public**, so the reasoning must survive being read by opponents
:::

## Which makes session 10 and 11 the centre of gravity

::: {.tight}
- Did the subsidy raise employment, or did healthier regions take up the subsidy?
- Did the regulation change behaviour, or was behaviour changing already?
- Would the trend have been parallel? **Say how you would probe it, not that you assumed it.**
:::

::: {.check}
In public work, "we could not identify this effect from these data" is not a failure to deliver.
It is often the single most valuable thing you can report.
:::

## Both sectors, one standard

Whether the reader is a CFO or a director general, the same three questions decide whether your
number survives contact with them:

::: {.step}
**What exactly is being claimed**, in units, with an interval?
:::

::: {.step}
**What has to be true** for that claim to hold?
:::

::: {.step}
**What would change your mind**, and would you notice if it happened?
:::

# 6 · What this course did not cover {background-color="#16181A" style="color:#F7F6F3"}

### Knowing the shape of the gap

## Five absences worth naming

::: {.tight}
- **Time series proper** — autocorrelation, unit roots, cointegration, forecasting. Our panels are
  short and wide; session 6 only gestures at it
- **Bayesian inference** — everything here is frequentist, and the Bayesian framing is often the
  more natural one for a decision problem
- **Machine learning at scale** — gradient boosting, random forests, neural networks. Session 8's
  framework is their foundation; the methods are a course of their own
- **Text, networks, unstructured data** — where much of the growth in this field now is
- **Causal machine learning** — double ML and causal forests sit exactly at the junction of
  sessions 5, 8 and 10, and are the natural next thing to read
:::

# 7 · What to carry {background-color="#16181A" style="color:#F7F6F3"}

### Six habits that outlast every technique here

## The six

::: {.tight}
1. **Look at the data before modelling it.** Nearly every analysis that goes wrong went wrong before
   the model was fitted.
2. **Say the units.** Checking against what you already know is the fastest way to catch an
   implausible result.
3. **Report the uncertainty, and say what kind.** Classical, robust, clustered — they differed by
   more than a factor of two on one coefficient in session 6.
4. **Name the assumption that identifies the estimate**, and say whether it is testable. Most of the
   important ones are not — which is exactly why they must be argued.
5. **Fit the simpler thing too.** Complexity should have to beat something.
6. **Say what the result does not license.**
:::

## And the one that contains them

::: {.tight}
A well-argued refusal is a complete result.
:::

"This cannot be claimed from these data, and here is what would be needed."

::: {.check}
That is often the most valuable output of a serious analysis — and the answer that takes the most
expertise to produce.
:::

# 8 · Europe 2031, one more time {background-color="#16181A" style="color:#F7F6F3"}

### The course opened with it. It closes with it.

## In session 1 you had no tools

You read *Europe 2031* and were asked to separate four kinds of statement that the text moves
between without announcing it.

| | |
|---|---|
| **Evidence** | A claim tied to a source and an observed period |
| **Scenario** | A coherent imagined future — not a forecast by default |
| **Prediction** | A dated, testable statement about an outcome |
| **AI** | A computational system producing outputs from inputs and learned parameters |

::: {.check}
Read it again this week. You will find seams you could not see in August.
:::

## It is an optimistic document

And that is a feature of it, not a flaw — a scenario is meant to make a future feel *thinkable*.

::: {.warn}
But the optimism is carried by the **assumptions**, not by the evidence. Several of them are
inflated, and a diagnosis built on inflated assumptions is sometimes simply wrong.
:::

## Take the compute assumption

The scenario assigns the United States roughly **12 times** Europe's AI compute stock in 2031, and
treats compute as the dominant measure of geopolitical capability.

::: {.tight}
- Where does the ratio come from — measured, or assumed?
- Is compute the right measure of capability, or the *available* one?
- What observation would count as **evidence against** it?
:::

::: {.check}
You now have the training to ask that in the form of a testable statement. In August you did not.
That is the distance you have travelled.
:::

## Actual AI is not the AI of the discourse

| The buzz | The thing itself |
|---|---|
| A system that "understands" | A function fitted to data, producing outputs from learned parameters |
| Reasoning, in the human sense | Very good conditional prediction over patterns it has seen |
| Improvement without limit | Improvement bounded by data, compute, and an irreducible error term |
| Ground truth | Confident output, whether or not the question was answerable |

::: {.warn}
Session 8's bias–variance decomposition applies to every one of these systems. The irreducible error
does not go away because the model got larger.
:::

## Which is the same lesson as week one

The model on your laptop does not refuse either. It answers fluently when it should not, exactly as
the normal equations do.

::: {.check}
The skill this course built — *knowing which question a given number can answer, and saying so when
it cannot* — is precisely the skill that the arrival of these systems has made **scarcer and more
valuable**, not less.
:::

## Where the work goes now

Language models have made the arithmetic and the code effectively free. They have **not** made the
judgement free, and there is no sign that they will.

::: {.tight}
That is the argument for learning to derive a method before using it. Not because the derivation
will be needed at the keyboard — but because it is what lets you notice that the answer on the
screen cannot be right.
:::

## Thank you

You arrived able to run a regression. You leave able to say what one is entitled to claim.

::: {.check}
That is a much rarer thing, and it is the whole point.
:::

*Europe 2031* · [europe2031.ai](https://europe2031.ai) — read it again, and mark the seams.

## Now, the last five groups

That was the last teaching of the course. What follows is not an epilogue to it — it is the
argument being made by you instead of me.

::: {.tight}
Same three questions, from the floor:
:::

::: {.step}
**What exactly is being claimed**, in units, with an interval?
:::

::: {.step}
**What has to be true** for that claim to hold?
:::

::: {.step}
**What would change your mind**, and would you notice if it happened?
:::
